Listen to this article Share Thousands of African graduates seeking employment in the United Kingdom (UK) could lose six months of post-study work opportunities under a new immigration policy that makes the duration of their stay dependent on the university they attend. The UK government will retain the two-year Graduate visa for international students completing degrees at selected universities, while graduates from other institutions will receive only 18 months from January 1, 2027. The arrangement creates a two-tier system in which a university’s immigration compliance record and graduate employment outcomes could determine how long international students can remain in Britain after graduation. The decision partially reverses an earlier plan to reduce the Graduate visa for all bachelor’s and master’s degree holders from two years to 18 months. However, the government has not disclosed which universities will qualify for the longer period or how their performance will be assessed. Read also: UK study visa crackdown: Nigeria, Pakistan bear brunt with withdrawals In its 2026 Budget, the government said the extended period would apply to graduates from institutions with strong immigration compliance records and positive employment outcomes. “The government will also increase the duration of the Graduate visa to two years for graduates from high compliance universities where there are strong labour market outcomes,” the Budget document stated. The policy has significant implications for African students, particularly Nigerians, who constitute a major segment of the UK’s international student population and often rely on post-study employment to gain professional experience and recover the cost of studying abroad. Nigeria was the UK’s third-largest source of sponsored international students in the year ending June 2026, with 26,060 study visas issued to Nigerian main applicants, behind China and India. Nigerians were also among the largest beneficiaries of the Graduate route, with 20,604 nationals receiving approval during the period, the third-highest figure among nationalities. The figures highlight the potential scale of the policy’s impact, although the number of African graduates affected extends beyond Nigeria. Read also: UK raises student visa proof of funds for Nigerians, others University choice becomes an immigration consideration The new arrangement means prospective international students may have to consider a university’s eligibility for the extended Graduate visa alongside tuition fees, academic reputation and employment prospects. For students financing their education through personal savings, family support or loans, losing six months of post-study work eligibility could reduce the time available to secure employment, gain experience and transition to a longer-term immigration route. The Graduate visa allows eligible international students to work or search for employment without first obtaining employer sponsorship. However, it cannot be extended, meaning graduates who wish to remain in Britain beyond its validity must qualify for another immigration category, such as the Skilled Worker visa. Under the revised rules, students graduating before the end of 2026 can still apply for the existing two-year Graduate visa. The shorter 18-month period will apply to applications submitted from January 1, 2027, while doctoral graduates will continue to qualify for three years. The absence of a published list of qualifying universities creates uncertainty for students making admission and financial decisions ahead of the implementation date. Without clear assessment criteria, prospective applicants may struggle to determine whether their chosen institution will provide access to the longer post-study period. Read also: Disappointment trails UK’s new policy on foreign student visa UK expands opportunities for highly skilled graduates Alongside the changes to the Graduate route, Britain plans to widen access to its High Potential Individual visa by extending eligibility to graduates of the world’s top 150 universities, compared with the smaller group currently covered. The route allows eligible graduates of leading overseas institutions to move to the UK without securing a job offer before arrival. The government also intends to give some highly skilled sponsored workers up to six months to find another job when their existing sponsorship ends. Together, the measures suggest a more selective approach to international migration. While the government is shortening the post-study work period for some graduates, it is creating additional opportunities for individuals from institutions and professional backgrounds it considers valuable to the British labour market.
